blocks.text: It is proved that חריונים, or דביונים, 2 Reg. VI, 25, is a kind of chickpea, not dove's dung, as has hitherto been believed.

It is related in 2 Reg. VI, 25 that in the time of the famine at Samaria רובע הקב חריונים, the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung, was sold for five pieces of silver. Understand by these silver coins half-ounce pieces, each worth about thirty-six Tours sous, so that the total came to roughly nine livres of our money. Further, all the Hebrews with complete agreement report that the cab held only twenty-four eggs. So the fourth part of a cab would be a log, that is, a measure of six eggs. I shall not undertake to prove these things, lest I seem to do what has already been done. I shall only try to answer a most difficult question, which no one has solved so far: why so tiny a measure of so worthless a thing, namely dove's dung, was valued so highly, and for what use it was bought.

I. There are those who say that the Samaritans, pressed by hunger, used this dung as food. Among them is Eutychius, patriarch of Alexandria, in his Annals, where he speaks of the famine of Samaria, p. 213: واكلوا زبل الحمام [wa-akalū zibl al-ḥamām] And they ate dove's dung. In the same way Rabshakeh, about to besiege Jerusalem, threatened that he would make the inhabitants eat their own dung and drink their own urine, 2 Reg. XVIII, 27, and Es. XXXVI, 12. But these words of Rabshakeh are nothing but the empty taunt of a boastful Thraso, by which he meant that the people of Jerusalem would be oppressed by the utmost want of all things. And the Hebrews rightly interpret the [col. 39] saying על דרך גוזמא, by way of hyperbole; for it is a thing without precedent that anyone should, like swine, have swallowed the dung of others, let alone his own. Nature utterly recoils from so monstrous a food. Or if, when famine struck, necessity bound with iron spikes drove someone to it, he would still do it in vain, because nothing remains in excrement that can be digested. This is far more true of dove's dung than of human dung, because it is much hotter. This is taught both by experience itself and by the books of the physicians and of all who have written on manuring. Varro, De re rust. book 1, ch. 38: Cassius writes that the best dung (for manuring fields) is that of birds, etc. Of these, that of doves is the best, because it is the hottest. Columella book 2, ch. 15: There are, then, three chief kinds of dung: that from birds, that from men, and that from cattle. Of birds' dung the first is held to be that which is cleared out of dovecotes. Pliny book 17, ch. 9: Marcus Varro gives first place to the dung of thrushes from aviaries. Columella puts that from dovecotes next, [II, 573] then that from henhouses. Some prefer that from dovecotes. Palladius book 2, ch. 33: That of doves (dung) is the most fiery, and that of other birds is quite useful. Quintilius book 2 of the Geopon.: Ἔστι δὲ κόπρος μὲν καλὴ ἡ τῶν πτηνῶν ἁπάντων, πλὴν τῶν χηνῶν, καὶ τῶν ἐνύδρων ὀρνέων, διὰ τὴν ὑγρότητα [esti de kopros men kalē hē tōn ptēnōn hapantōn, plēn tōn chēnōn, kai tōn enydrōn orneōn, dia tēn hygrotēta], etc. Πολὺ δὲ καλλίων ἡ τῶν περιστερῶν, πολὺ τὸ θερμὸν ἔχουσα [poly de kalliōn hē tōn peristerōn, poly to thermon echousa]· The dung of all birds is good, except that of geese and water-birds, because of its moisture, etc. but that of doves is far superior, because it is the most fiery. Avicenna book 2 of the Canon, in the chapter زبل [zibl], or On dung: زبل الحمام اسخان الازبال المستعمل [zibl al-ḥamām askhan al-azbāl al-mustaʿmal] Dove's dung is the hottest of all those that have any use. The cause is clear from Aristotle, who lists the dove first among those that have θερμὴν κοιλίαν [thermēn koilian], a hotter stomach, De part. anim. book 2, ch. 7. Accordingly some of the moderns write that the dove, like the ostrich, swallows and digests small stones. And the Arabic name of the dove, حمام [ḥamām] himam, is formed from heat. These things, I think, show abundantly that nothing remains in dove's dung that a human being could digest ^{(1)}.
